question_en: Which of the following most likely benefits a trader who is short a put option?
option_a: A decrease in the price of the underlying asset
option_b: An increase in the price of the underlying asset
option_c: An increase in the volatility of the underlying asset
explanation_en: Options are contingent claims that give contract holders the right to trade the underlying asset at a specified price at a future date. That right may or may not have value at expiration. Option holders do not have to exercise their rights, but if they do, the original contract sellers are obligated to take the other side of the trade that results from the option exercise. For put options: the buyer (ie, holder) has the right to sell the underlying asset at the option's strike price, and the seller is obligated to buy the underlying asset at the strike price if the put holder exercises the option. An option seller's maximal potential profit is the price (ie, option premium) received for selling the option. That outcome is realized only if the option expires unexercised. A put holder will not exercise the right to sell at the strike price if the underlying asset can be sold at a higher market price (ie, the put is out of the money). Therefore, a put seller benefits when the price of the underlying asset increases since that increases the probability that the put option will not be exercised. (Choices A and C) A decrease in the underlying asset's price or an increase in its price volatility increases the value of a put option. The value of a short put position is adversely affected by an increase in the put's value.

question_en: An equity call option is most likely in the money when the stock price is greater than the:
option_c: present value of the strike price.
explanation_en: Moneyness Call Condition Put In the money Spot price > Strike price Out of the money At the money Spot price = Strike price At the money Out of the money Spot price < Strike price In the money Options are contingent claims that give holders (ie, buyer or long party) the right to trade an underlying asset at a fixed price (ie, strike or exercise price) at a future date. In the money means that an option has value if exercised: the option allows the holder to trade the underlying at a better price than its current market price. Calls are in the money when the asset's market price is > the option's exercise price. Puts are in the money when the asset's market price is < the option's exercise price. If an equity call is in the money, the option holder can buy the underlying stock through exercise of the option at a lower price than it would cost to buy the shares in the open market. (Choice B) The underlying stock price needs to be above a call's strike price plus premium (ie, breakeven point) for the call buyer to earn a profit. However, moneyness is determined by the relationship of the underlying asset's price to the exercise price, regardless of the premium paid. (Choice C) The present value of the strike price is used in option valuation (eg, put-call parity) but is not a factor in determining an option's moneyness.

explanation_en: Underlying asset price volatility is directly related to both call and put values. Greater asset price volatility may place the option further in the money or out of the money. Representative price ranges for low-volatility and high-volatility asset prices are shown in the image above. If an option is in the money, its value is positive, and further favorable price movement increases its value (ie, it will be further in the money). If an option is out of the money, its value is zero, and further adverse price movement does not decrease its value (ie, its value is bounded by zero). Although the image above illustrates volatility's effect on calls only, all contingent claims have asymmetric value profiles; therefore, both call and put values are directly related to volatility (Choices B and C).

question_en: Which of the following transactions best replicates a long European call option?
option_a: Buying a put and a share of stock and selling a zero-coupon bond
option_b: Buying a zero-coupon bond and selling a put and a share of stock
option_c: Buying a share of stock and selling a put and a zero-coupon bond
explanation_en: Put-call parity is a concept that describes a relationship between the prices of a European call and a European put, both of which have the same exercise (strike) price and expiration. Put and call options can be used to create portfolios that produce identical payoffs. As shown above, a put option can be combined with a share of stock, which is known as a protective put. A fiduciary call consists of a call option and the present value of a zero-coupon bond that has a face value equal to the option's strike price. Since the price of the stock and the present value of the bond can be observed directly, the options must be priced to prevent arbitrage opportunities. Rearranging the formula demonstrates that any variable can be replicated with a combination of long and short positions in the three remaining variables. For instance, one can replicate a long call option by buying a put, buying a share of stock, and selling a zero-coupon bond: If the market price of the put is known, inserting it into the right side of the equation produces the expected price of the call. If it differs from the call's actual market price, an arbitrage opportunity exists. (Choice B) This combination creates a short position in a call option. (Choice C) Put-call parity does not allow this combination of assets.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.09 Option Replication Using Put–Call Parity - Answers.pdf
question_en: A portfolio consists of a protective put position. For put-call parity to hold, a portfolio of equal value most appropriately consists of a call with the same strike and expiration as the put and:
option_b: a long position in the underlying asset.
option_c: a short position in the underlying asset.
explanation_en: Put-call parity forms the foundation of put-call-forward parity. Put-call parity asserts that a protective put and fiduciary call constructed with European options on the same underlying asset and with the same strike price and expiration have the same payoff; therefore, at any time prior to maturity the values of the protective put and fiduciary call are equal. In put-call-forward parity the protective put portfolio is created by replacing the underlying with an equivalent synthetic asset (S). The synthetic asset consists of a long forward contract and a risk-free zero-coupon bond with a face value equal to the asset's forward price. Entering into a forward contract costs nothing, so the value of the synthetic asset at Time 0 is simply the zero-coupon bond's present value. At expiration, the value of the maturing zero-coupon bond could be used to purchase the underlying asset by exercising the forward contract. (Choice A) The forward contract does not replace the risk-free bond. In fact, it requires the addition of a risk-free bond to the protective put portfolio. (Choice B) The forward contract is part of the protective put portfolio, not the fiduciary call portfolio. Therefore, the forward contract does not replace the strike price of the call option.

explanation_en: Put-call parity is a concept that describes a relationship between the prices of a European call and a European put, both of which have the same exercise (strike) price and expiration. Since the price of the stock and the present value of the bond can be observed directly, the options must be priced to prevent arbitrage opportunities. question_en: An investor finds that a forward price is greater than the price implied by put-call parity. To earn a risk-free profit, the investor should most likely sell the forward contract, buy risk-free bonds, and:
option_a: buy a call and sell a put.
option_b: sell a call and buy a put.
option_c: buy a call and buy a put.
explanation_en:
According to put-call parity, protective puts and fiduciary calls constructed with options on the same asset with the same strike price and expiry
generate equal payoffs. Therefore, at any time prior to expiration, the value of these economically equivalent portfolios should be equal. Any
mispricing compared to values implied by put-call parity results in arbitrage trading, which forces all elements of the equivalent portfolios to
ultimately trade at relative fair value.
Synthetic asset positions can be created with forward contracts and risk-free bonds. Arbitrage pricing applies to put-call-forward parity when the
asset in the protective put portfolio is replaced by the synthetic asset.
If any component is mispriced, risk-free profits can be earned by selling the relatively overpriced component and buying its synthetic equivalent,
or vice versa. In this scenario, that entails selling the relatively overpriced forward contract and going long its synthetic equivalent. A synthetic
long forward position implies buying the call and selling the put.
Note: The signs in the formula generally indicate the appropriate positioning or action; + means long or buy and − means short or sell.
(Choice B) Selling a call and buying a put (ie, synthetic short forward contract) is appropriate for arbitrage if a forward contract is priced below fair
value.
(Choice C) Arbitrage to profit from relative mispricing requires opposite trades (ie, buying one and selling the other) in puts and calls; therefore,
buying both puts and calls is not the appropriate action in this scenario.

question_en: According to put-call-forward parity, which of the following combinations of positions most appropriately replicates a short position in a forward contract?
option_a: Short a call option, long a put option, and long a risk-free bond
option_b: Long a call option, short a put option, and long a risk-free bond
option_c: Short a call option, long a put option, and short a risk-free bond
explanation_en:
Replication combines assets and/or derivatives to create a position that produces the same cash flows or characteristics as a different
asset. Replication enforces the no-arbitrage condition: Functionally identical positions must be priced identically, or an investor could earn riskless
profits (ie, arbitrage) by exploiting the mispricing of the two positions.
Replication can be accomplished with put-call-forward parity. The diagram above shows that a forward contract is identical to being:
long a European call option with exercise price X that expires at time t,
short a European put option with exercise price X that expires at time t, and
long a risk-free zero-coupon bond with face value X that matures at time t.
A short position in the forward price is replicated by multiplying the call-put-bond position by −1, which results in being short the call option, long
the put, and short the bond:
(Choice A) Being short a call option, long a put option, and long a risk-free bond replicates no position in put-call-forward parity.
(Choice B) Under put-call-forward parity, being long a call option, short a put option, and long a risk-free bond replicates a long position in a
forward contract.
